body.text: As it heads into the crucial midterm elections — effectively a referendum on the president and his party — the United States is facing a series of health crises. Healthcare costs are ballooning, reproductive health and abortion services have been compromised, assistance for the LGBTQI community is being cut, preventable infectious diseases are breaking out, food safety concerns have intensified, healthcare workforce shortages are growing and climate change’s health effects are being ignored.

Healthcare costs are a top worry for voters, and polling by the KFF health policy centre shows Democrats holding a twenty-point advantage over Republicans on the issue. Yet Donald Trump and health secretary Robert F. Kennedy are doubling down on costly, poorly evidenced policies and rhetoric.

Trump continues to promise a great healthcare plan but has yet to produce more than sketchy “concepts.” The most concrete of these, his most-favoured-nation drug pricing policy, has been severely eroded by widespread exemptions and now faces a lawsuit from the pharmaceutical lobby; in its present form it will do little to lower prices for patients or reduce federal spending on medicines.

Recognising voters’ concerns, Trump has been sending cheques to millions of Medicare and Affordable Care Act enrolees. But poll after poll reveals that Americans view this for what it is — a vote-buying stunt that does nothing to relieve healthcare costs.

America’s healthcare is the most expensive in the world. Despite its cutting-edge medical research and innovation, the country consistently lags behind high-income nations in health status and life expectancy. This highly inefficient system leaves a third of Americans “very worried” about their ability to pay for medications, doctor’s visits, health insurance or an unpredictably costly medical emergency.

Adding to the problem is the trillion dollars of healthcare cuts in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which have deprived millions of Americans of health insurance and food assistance. The “big, ugly bill,” as Democrats call it, is expected to drive another ten million people off health insurance by 2034. The “Medicare-for-All” message disseminated by Democratic progressives is consequently resonating with voters. Trump might label single-payer proposals as costly socialist schemes but fully two-thirds of Americans now favour some form of Medicare-for-All.

Health status and longevity are influenced by long-term social, economic and medical developments, so we can’t yet measure the impact of Trump 2.0. But Trumpism’s blizzard of poorly evidenced change is unlikely to bring good news. Budget and staffing cutbacks and the undermining of expertise in key health agencies and their expert advisory groups — the Food and Drug Administration, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or CDC, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices — are already having serious adverse consequences.

Measles is resurgent in several states. The Pennsylvania outbreak, which has taken five lives, is the state’s largest surge since 1991. New York has just declared a disaster emergency as its case numbers rise. CDC data indicate that 95 per cent of measles cases in 2026 were in children and adults who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown. The United States has not yet lost its measles elimination status (held since 2000), but its loss is expected after a formal review by the Pan American Health Organization scheduled for later this month.

Thousands of Americans, mostly children, are paying the price for scepticism about vaccination. Kennedy, who for years has made unproven claims about the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, has finally conceded its importance. “I’ve never questioned the efficacy of the MMR vaccine,” he said in a CNN interview in August. “A measles vaccine is effective. It stops measles in about 97 per cent of the cases.”

He was being disingenuous. At the recent Make America Healthy Again summit he questioned how the states and the media report measles deaths and contrasted public concern over measles with what he characterised as a lack of concern about alleged vaccine injuries. And just a week after Kennedy urged parents to vaccinate their children, Trump signed an executive order calling for the MMR to be split into smaller shots. The vaccine could be “quite lethal” if given all at once, he claimed, comparing it to pouring a bottle of soda into a child’s body.

Under Kennedy, the CDC has stopped recommending six routine childhood vaccines, including those that protect against hepatitis B, respiratory syncytial virus and meningitis. More deaths are an inevitable consequence. The hepatitis B shot for American newborns, for example, had dramatically reduced childhood infections from around 18,000 cases a year (about half of these at birth) to fewer than 1000 (with only twenty babies infected at birth).

Small wonder most Americans are confused about the administration’s stance on vaccines. In Texas, meanwhile, the Republican attorney-general is threatening action against paediatricians he claims are coercing parents into vaccinating their children. Undoing this confusion and distrust will require a huge long-term effort.

Cuts to regulations and regulatory agencies are also making food contamination problems increasingly common. Earlier this year thousands were sickened by a multistate outbreak of Cyclospora infections linked to iceberg lettuce and jalapenos from central Mexico. Federal agencies were slow to respond and state and local health departments bore the immediate weight of tracking, interviewing patients and identifying regional clusters.

Also this year, major food recalls have targeted eggs (due to Salmonella contamination), blueberries (E. coli) and a number of dairy products (Listeria). A 2025 study shows that foodborne illnesses cost Americans an estimated US$75 billion a year in medical care, lost productivity and premature deaths; yet the Trump administration has reduced active surveillance through FoodNet, compromising the public health system’s ability to detect early signals of emerging problems.

Rising temperatures, shifting eco-systems and a lack of surveillance and reporting have allowed ticks and mosquitoes to thrive where they could not previously survive. With deer ticks now found much further north and active for longer, Lyme disease is exploding, with more than 500,000 cases predicted for 2026. Mosquito-borne diseases are increasing, with a dengue fever outbreak in Florida and widespread activity of West Nile virus across multiple states.

These diseases have not been entirely ignored by the administration, but its response has been decidedly ideological, if not weird. Kennedy has made Lyme disease one of his priorities in office, claiming that “Americans can’t go into the woods any more safely” because of the disease. In the past, he has said Lyme disease is “highly likely to have been a military weapon.” More recently, he said he believes Lyme disease was “almost certainly” the result of gain-of-function research.

And while Trump is fulminating about the Russian lab leak of plague bacteria that has reportedly claimed two lives, a woman in New Mexico died from plague in June; Arizona had reported a pneumonic plague-related death last year. As many as seventeen cases of plague (a disease caused by the Yersinia pestis bacterium transmitted by fleas that live on rodents) are reported in the United States each year, mostly in New Mexico, California and Colorado.

Donald Trump and his cabinet have been particularly dismissive of the health risks of climate change, which they describe as a “scam.” The Environmental Protection Agency has abolished emission limits for coal- and gas-fired power plants and rolled back motor vehicle standards, but the impacts on disease spread and health are growing.

Valley fever, caused by a soil-dwelling fungus, is a prime example. It is spreading from rural areas in the southwestern states into urban California, driven by climate patterns and soil disruption caused by dust storms and oil drilling. Researchers estimate that between 205,000 and 360,000 symptomatic cases occur annually — far higher than official counts. Trump claims the 2009 scientific conclusion that greenhouse gas emissions pose a danger to Americans’ health and welfare “had no basis in fact.” But the added pollution following the repeal of an EPA determination could cause up to 58,000 premature deaths and an increase of thirty-seven million asthma attacks between now and 2055.

Perhaps the biggest and most immediate impacts on Americans’ health have resulted from Trump’s commitment to MAGA-inspired policies on reproductive health and abortion, diversity, equity and inclusion, and immigration.

Overturning the federally recognised right to abortion and subsequent moves by many Republican states to dramatically limit abortion rights have had awful consequences for maternal and child health. In Texas, for example, where access to abortion is severely limited, infant deaths have increased, partly driven by an increase in babies with birth defects.

Facing clinical hesitation and legal fear, doctors and hospitals in restricted states are often delaying critical miscarriage management and emergency obstetric care. Clinic closures following total or partial bans on abortion and reduced access to healthcare funding have left millions of women with a severe dearth of obstetric and gynaecologic providers. Low-income women, rural residents, and communities of colour face the steepest travel barriers, higher uninsured rates, and compounding healthcare disparities when trying to access out-of-state care.

Trump has taken numerous healthcare-related executive actions. His administration has finalised a rule, due to be implemented this month, to end gender-affirming care through Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program, a move that will make it harder for vulnerable children to access treatment and care. This new rule is subject to legal challenges that could delay or block it entirely. Additionally, the Department of Health and Human Services has targeted more than 250 healthcare entities providing gender-affirming care to minors “for investigation into possible violation of federal statutes.” This has led to dozens of major providers abruptly ceasing care provision. A federal judge blocked the administration from pursuing this prosecution in a decision that chastised Kennedy for his “wanton disregard” for the law that “causes very real harm to very real people.”

Federal agency layoffs, funding and reimbursement cuts and restructures have all reduced worker numbers. Arrests and deportations have disrupted care for some patients, and fears of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, officials have caused patients to delay needed care. Experts are projecting that Trump’s policies will exacerbate staff shortages, especially in long-term care where roughly 30 per cent of workers are immigrants.

All in all, it’s a grim outlook if Trump’s policies are maintained. It is shocking how recent progress in improving health status can be turned back in so short a time, with so little thought for the long-term costs. It seems increasingly likely that Americans will imagine Trump on the ballot — as he has requested — and vote against Republican candidates, and for better health and healthcare, in November. •
